extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and literary practitioners (classical/educated audience seeking guidance on poetic craft and patronage)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and ethical guidance for composing poetry and drama and for managing social relations with patrons and readers in a classical literary career. Covers craft (originality, emotional effect, avoidance of cheap popular tricks), professional etiquette (how to present work, accept criticism), and patronage tactics (tact, discretion, recommendations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality in material while learning forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt forms and metres from models (e.g., iambics, Archilochus' rhythm) but do not copy their words or content slavishly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established metres and structures as tools ('Following Archilochus in rhythm and stave'), yet supply new thoughts and language so that your work is not mere verbal imitation. Example anti-pattern: reproducing the exact diction of a predecessor even when using the same rhythmic pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering to popular applause or spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not stoop to win the rabble's votes by cheap tricks, shows, or stage finery; favor substance over vulgar attractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace criticizes those who seek crowd-pleasing through refreshments, costumes, and spectacular stage effects rather than through strong writing. In drama, beware of relying on chariots, animals, or dazzling props that distract from the author’s voice ('That woollen mantle with the violet dye'). Anti-pattern: writing to elicit immediate noisy applause at the expense of artistic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to move the reader/audience (emotional effectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true master is one who can with fictitious woes wring, rouse, soothe, and pierce the reader — to evoke genuine feeling and transport the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essential test of success is the poem's power to affect emotions and imagination ('bear me to Thebes, to Athens'). Prioritize emotional truth and imaginative transport over mere technical display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on age or death to legitimate work
rubrics_metrics.description: Value and judge poetry by its intrinsic merit rather than by how long it has existed or whether the author is dead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace mocks the notion that time alone confers greatness and warns against using 'death' or longevity as a criterion for worth. Evaluate works critically on quality rather than antiquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge works on merit, not ancient reputation alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist uncritical reverence for ancient poets; some old works are rough or defective and should not be elevated blindly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the default assumption that antiquity equals perfection; recognize that earlier works may be incomplete or hasty. Anti-pattern: refusing to criticize an ancient author simply because they are old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect craft and skill — not all may write well
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledges that skilled craftsmen should handle specialized tasks (as with tools or medicine), and that poetry requires learned skill rather than undisciplined scribbling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace notes a tension: while everyone may scribble verses, true poetry is a craft requiring training and judgement. Encourage disciplined learning and technical competence; avoid vanity-writing without skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intrusive self-promotion and social badgering
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pester friends or audiences by repeatedly reciting unasked passages, expecting instant praise, or intruding on their time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace counsels poets not to force their work on others, to accept criticism rather than demand praise, and not to re-recite passages unrequested. Anti-pattern: overbearing behaviour that alienates potential patrons and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write appropriate work for your intended medium (readers vs. theatre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between writing to be read and writing to be acted; each medium demands different priorities (e.g., subtle diction for reading, presence for stage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who write to be read should furnish 'worthy gear' for the bookish audience; dramatists must contend with noisy crowds and theatrical competition. Tailor technique and content to the audience and venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer substance and dignity to frivolous or derivative themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Select subject matter and treatment that sustain dignity and strength rather than relying on trivial popular motifs or mere novelty-of-style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace praises works that avoid triviality and achieve noble effect; he warns against themes that aim only to dazzle temporarily and then are forgotten.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and learn from criticism; cultivate modesty and persistence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not resent corrective remarks; use criticism and sage conversation to refine your sense of what procures peace, curbs desire, and elevates virtue in life and art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace urges dialogue with sages, questions about moderation, and self-culture as part of a poet's development. Anti-pattern: taking offence or expecting immediate laurels instead of steady improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse independence with boorishness; avoid flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a balanced comportment between servile flattery and crude independence; neither constant sycophancy nor deliberate rudeness is virtuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace contrasts the professional flatterer (parasite) with the boor who prides himself on brutal frankness — both are faults. Virtue lies between extremes: be tactful but not obsequious; honest but not rude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tact in seeking patrons (mask need, show competence)
rubrics_metrics.description: When courting the favour of great men, those who can conceal pressing need and show worth politely win more than plaintive beggars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace advises that modest behaviour, controlled displays of ability, and avoiding plaintive whining are more effective in gaining patrons than begging or aggressive demands. Example: mask poverty modestly rather than loudly plead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard confidences and choose what to reveal and to whom
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid careless prying and the practice of broadcasting what you learn; wide ears don't keep secrets and may betray you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be discreet about private matters, especially when they concern patrons or recommendations. Anti-patterns include indiscriminate gossip and constant questioning that spreads secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet recommendations and protégés carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Look round and judge the person you recommend; the recommender bears shame if the protege offends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a protege proves unworthy through his own fault, it may be wiser to abandon him and back a known, proven candidate instead. Recommendation is a responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate behaviour to fit company; avoid extremes in public persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid appearing crabbed by too much silence or obscure by excessive modesty; be socially adaptable in manner and conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace warns that the silent man may be judged crabbed and the excessively modest obscure; cultivate a temperate public comportment appropriate to contexts such as feasts, hunts, or discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let theatrical mob or spectacle dictate artistic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Because theatrical audiences are noisy and easily dazzled by foreign finery and stagecraft, playwrights must not let that low standard be the sole measure of dramatic worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace dissects how scenes and stagecraft can mask poor writing; dramatists should preserve voice and textual strength that can survive the theatre's distractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate integrity and virtue as foundations for reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: True 'good' consists in love of right and upright conduct, not merely outward compliance with laws and ceremonies; integrity cannot be faked by appearances alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace contrasts mere formal goodness with inner rectitude; for poets and public figures alike, reputation rests better on real virtue than on performative acts. Anti-pattern: relying on outward legalistic behaviour while harbouring corrupt motives.
